title: Introduction to Minimum Spanning Tree (Kruskal)
description: Build the cheapest tree connecting all nodes by greedily adding the smallest safe edges

blocks.text: A minimum spanning tree, or MST, is the cheapest way to connect every node of a weighted graph together, using no more edges than necessary. Kruskal algorithm is one of the two classic ways to build it.
Kruskal is beautifully simple: sort all the edges from cheapest to most expensive, then add them one by one, skipping any edge that would form a cycle. That greedy sweep produces the optimal tree.

blocks.caption: A weighted graph whose cheapest connecting tree we want to find
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655778-815815439.png

By the end of this topic you will understand what an MST is, the greedy idea behind Kruskal, how union find detects cycles, the full algorithm and code, why the greedy choice is provably optimal, and how Kruskal compares with Prim. It is a cornerstone of graph algorithms.
If you have already met union find, Kruskal will feel like its natural application. In fact Kruskal is the classic reason union find is worth learning in the first place.
Keep the greedy spirit in mind throughout: always grab the cheapest edge that safely connects something new.

content.title: 1. What is a Minimum Spanning Tree?

blocks.text: Start with a connected, weighted, undirected graph. A spanning tree is a selection of edges that connects all the nodes together and contains no cycle. For n nodes, a spanning tree always has exactly n minus 1 edges.

blocks.caption: A spanning tree connects every node with no cycle; the MST minimises total weight
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655778-433035980.png
blocks.alt: What is a Minimum Spanning Tree?

blocks.text: Among all the possible spanning trees, the minimum spanning tree is the one whose edge weights add up to the smallest total. It is the cheapest possible way to keep everything connected.

items: The graph is connected, weighted, and undirected
A spanning tree connects all nodes with no cycle
It always uses exactly n minus 1 edges for n nodes
The MST is the spanning tree with the least total weight

blocks.text:
Not always unique:

A graph can have several minimum spanning trees if some edge weights tie. They all share the same minimum total weight, which is what matters.
The word spanning captures the requirement that the tree reaches every node, and tree captures that it has no cycle and uses the fewest possible edges.

items: Connected: every node is reachable
Acyclic: no cycles, so it is a true tree
Spanning: it includes all n nodes
Minimum: the total edge weight is as small as possible

blocks.text: The MST answers a very practical question: what is the cheapest set of connections that keeps a whole network joined together?
That question shows up constantly in the real world, wherever you must link everything while spending as little as possible on the links themselves.

items: Laying the least cable to connect a set of buildings
Designing a road or pipeline network at minimum cost
Clustering data by connecting nearest points cheaply
Approximating harder routing problems

blocks.text: In every case the goal is the same shape: connect everyone, add no redundant links, and keep the total cost as low as possible. That is exactly what an MST gives you.
The common thread is a tradeoff between connectivity and cost. You must keep the network whole, but every extra or expensive link wastes money.
An MST resolves that tradeoff exactly: full connectivity for the least total cost, with not a single redundant edge.
Kruskal takes the most natural greedy approach imaginable. If you want cheap total weight, you should prefer cheap edges, so consider the edges in order of increasing weight.

blocks.caption: Sort edges by weight, then add each one that connects two separate components
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655778-864589261.png

Sweep through the sorted edges from cheapest to most expensive. For each edge, add it to your tree if it connects two pieces that were not yet connected. If both of its endpoints are already in the same connected piece, adding it would create a cycle, so skip it.
You keep going until you have added n minus 1 edges, at which point every node is connected and the tree is complete. That is the entire algorithm in one idea.

Greedy and correct:

Always taking the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle feels too simple to be optimal, yet it provably produces a minimum spanning tree every time.
Notice how local the decision is. Kruskal never looks ahead; it only asks whether the current cheapest edge connects two separate pieces.

items: Consider edges from cheapest to most expensive
Add an edge only if it joins two components
Skip any edge whose ends are already connected
Finish once n minus 1 edges have been chosen

blocks.text: The first concrete step is to gather all the edges and sort them by weight, smallest first. This ordering is what makes the greedy sweep possible.

Because we process edges strictly in increasing weight, whenever we accept an edge we know it is the cheapest available option that still helps connect the graph. The sorting is also the most expensive part of the whole algorithm.

items: Collect every edge as a triple of weight and its two endpoints
Sort the list by weight, smallest first
Process edges strictly in this order
Sorting dominates the running time

blocks.text: Any correct sort works, and the tie breaking between equal weights does not matter, since all minimum spanning trees share the same total.
This is also why Kruskal loves an edge list input: the edges are already in exactly the form the sort needs.

content.title: 5. The Cycle Problem and Union Find

blocks.text: The one tricky part is deciding, quickly, whether an edge would create a cycle. An edge creates a cycle exactly when both of its endpoints are already in the same connected group.

blocks.caption: An edge whose endpoints are already connected would form a cycle, so it is skipped
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655778-760718041.png
blocks.alt: The Cycle Problem and Union Find

blocks.text: To track which nodes are connected, Kruskal uses the union find data structure, also called disjoint set union. It keeps nodes grouped into components and answers two questions fast: which group is this node in, and merge these two groups.

items: An edge forms a cycle when both ends share a component
Union find tracks the current components
The find operation reports a node component
The union operation merges two components

blocks.text:
Why union find fits perfectly:

Kruskal only ever asks are these two nodes already connected, and please connect them. Those are exactly the two operations union find makes nearly constant time.
Without a fast way to test connectivity, checking each edge for a cycle would be slow. Union find is what keeps that test almost free.

items: find(x) returns the representative of a node component
unite(a, b) merges two components into one
Path compression flattens the structure over time
Union by rank or size keeps the trees shallow

content.title: 6. The Kruskal Algorithm Step by Step

blocks.text: Putting the pieces together gives a short, clear procedure.

blocks.caption: Add the cheapest edges in order, skipping any that would close a cycle
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761239-758856942.png
blocks.alt: The Kruskal Algorithm Step by Step

items: Sort all edges by weight, smallest first
Start with every node in its own component
For each edge in order, if its endpoints are in different components, add it and merge them
If its endpoints are already connected, skip the edge
Stop once you have added n minus 1 edges

blocks.text: Trace it on a tiny graph. Take edges of weight 1 and 2 first, skip a weight 4 edge because it would close a cycle, then take a weight 3 edge to finish. Three edges connect four nodes, and the MST is done.
Because we take edges in increasing order, the very first edge we accept is the cheapest in the whole graph, and every later acceptance is the cheapest that still connects something new.
The stopping rule is exact: a spanning tree of n nodes needs precisely n minus 1 edges, so we can quit the moment we reach that count.
The implementation is a union find structure plus a sorted sweep over the edges.

codes.python:
def kruskal(n, edges):                 # edges: list of (weight, u, v)
    parent = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x
    edges.sort()
    total = used = 0
    for w, u, v in edges:
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru != rv:                    # different components: safe to add
            parent[ru] = rv
            total += w
            used += 1
            if used == n - 1:
                break
    return total

blocks.text: The union find keeps each connectivity check nearly constant time, so after the initial sort the sweep is very fast.
The DSU find uses path compression so repeated lookups get faster, and unite refuses to merge two nodes already in the same set, which is exactly the cycle test.
Everything after the sort is close to linear, so the sort truly is the bottleneck.
It is worth knowing why such a simple greedy rule is guaranteed to be optimal. The reason is the cut property of minimum spanning trees.

The cut property says that for any way of splitting the nodes into two sides, the cheapest edge crossing that split is always safe to include in some MST. Kruskal, by always taking the cheapest edge that joins two different components, is repeatedly applying exactly this safe choice.

items: The cut property guarantees the cheapest crossing edge is safe
Kruskal always adds the cheapest edge joining two components
That edge crosses the cut between those components
So every edge Kruskal adds is a provably safe MST edge

blocks.text:
The intuition:

You never regret taking the cheapest edge that connects something new. A more expensive edge could always replace it later without ever helping, so the greedy pick is always safe.
Another way to see it is the exchange argument: if an optimal tree lacked our cheapest crossing edge, we could swap that edge in and a costlier one out without increasing the total.
Since the swap never makes things worse, some optimal tree always contains the greedy edge, which is what safety means.
Kruskal cost is dominated by sorting the edges, since everything after that is nearly linear.

items: Sorting the edges: O(E log E), the main cost
The union find operations: nearly O(E) in total, effectively constant per operation
Overall: O(E log E), or equivalently O(E log V)
Space: O(V) for the union find plus O(E) for the edge list

blocks.text: Because it is driven by the edges, Kruskal is especially natural when the graph is given as an edge list and is relatively sparse.
For a graph with V nodes and E edges, log E and log V differ only by a constant factor, so the bound is often written either way.
The near constant union find cost means the algorithm is, for practical purposes, just the cost of sorting the edges.
Kruskal and Prim both find a minimum spanning tree, but they grow it in different ways, and each suits different graphs.

items: Kruskal grows a forest, adding the globally cheapest safe edge each time, using union find
Prim grows one tree outward from a start node, always adding the cheapest edge leaving the tree, using a heap
Kruskal shines on sparse graphs given as an edge list
Prim shines on dense graphs where an adjacency structure is natural

blocks.text: They reach the same total weight; the choice is about the graph representation and density, not correctness.
A quick rule of thumb: reach for Kruskal when edges are few and already listed, and reach for Prim when the graph is dense and stored as adjacency lists.
Both are greedy and both are optimal, so the decision is purely about efficiency on your particular graph.
Minimum spanning trees, and Kruskal in particular, appear across many domains.

items: Designing least cost networks of cable, road, or pipe
Clustering, by building an MST and cutting its most expensive edges
Approximation algorithms for harder tour and routing problems
Image segmentation and other connectivity based grouping

blocks.text: The clustering use is especially elegant: build the MST, then remove the k most expensive edges to leave k natural clusters.
The same MST also gives a cheap backbone that other algorithms build on, such as approximations for the traveling salesman tour.
In clustering, the largest MST edges are the natural boundaries between groups, which makes cutting them a clean way to form clusters.

content.title: 12. Pitfalls and How to Approach It

blocks.text: Keep these points in mind to apply Kruskal correctly.

items: Remember an MST has exactly n minus 1 edges, so stop once you reach that many
Use union find with path compression, or the cycle checks become slow
On a disconnected graph, Kruskal yields a minimum spanning forest, not a single tree
Watch for integer overflow when summing many large edge weights

blocks.text:
How to spot an MST problem:

Look for connect everything at the lowest total cost with no redundant links. That phrasing almost always means a minimum spanning tree.
A frequent slip is forgetting that a disconnected input cannot have a spanning tree at all; Kruskal then produces a spanning forest, one tree per component.

Sum with care:

With many large weights, the total can exceed a 32 bit range. Use a 64 bit accumulator to avoid a silent overflow.
Kruskal is the greedy, edge driven way to build a minimum spanning tree.

items: An MST connects all nodes with n minus 1 edges at the least total weight
Kruskal sorts edges by weight and adds each one that does not form a cycle
Union find detects cycles by tracking connected components
It runs in O(E log E), dominated by the sort
The cut property is what makes the greedy choice provably optimal

blocks.text: Whenever you need the cheapest way to connect everything, sort the edges, sweep with union find, and Kruskal hands you the optimal tree.
